clue.text: Kay Boyle's Chekhovian bird

parts.note: Chekhov named a play after a shore bird, and the American writer Kay Boyle used the same bird in a story title

explanation.definitionFit: Chekhov's play about Nina and Trigorin is named for a coastal bird, the title Kay Boyle echoed.

clue.text: Papers disguised novelist's pen name

indicators.note: letters in disguise are dressed up differently, so the word papers is rearranged

explanation.surface: Some documents have been doctored to hide the pseudonym of a writer.
explanation.walkthrough: The pen name is that of H. C. McNeile, creator of Bulldog Drummond; 'disguised' fits a pseudonym neatly.
explanation.definitionFit: H. C. McNeile, an army engineer, wrote his thrillers under this military nickname as a pseudonym.

clue.text: A little air to be provided for singer

definitions.text: A little air to be provided for singer

parts.words: A little air to be provided for singer
parts.note: a short tune is a little air, and such a piece is written to be sung by a vocalist

explanation.definitionFit: A short operatic song is a diminutive of the Italian word for a solo melody.

clue.text: Free new Kahn's clue

indicators.note: making something new reworks it, so these letters are put in a fresh order

parts.note: the name with its S taken as letters
taken as written

explanation.surface: A fresh crossword hint from a setter named Kahn has been released.
explanation.definitionFit: To free a prisoner is to take off the fetters, a verb meaning release.

clue.text: A minor character of Swift

parts.note: minor reads as a lesser figure, but means tiny: Swift's Gulliver meets a race of very small people

explanation.definitionFit: Gulliver's Travels describes a land of people six inches tall, so any inhabitant is literally minor.

clue.text: Rehashed edibles provided for French composer

indicators.note: a rehash cooks up old food again, so the word edibles is reworked into a new order

explanation.surface: Leftover food is warmed up again for a musician from France.
explanation.walkthrough: Léo Delibes wrote the ballet Coppélia and the opera Lakmé.
explanation.definitionFit: Léo Delibes was the nineteenth-century Frenchman who wrote Coppélia and Lakmé.

clue.text: Elizabeth Bowen's was in the dark

definitions.text: Elizabeth Bowen's was in the dark

parts.words: Elizabeth Bowen's was in the dark
parts.note: Elizabeth Bowen published a story collection whose title puts a span of time in the dark

explanation.definitionFit: Bowen's collection is titled A ___ in the Dark, the gap filled by a twenty-four hour period.

clue.text: Mr Geller in a pound-to-a penny situation like the stuff of melodrama

indicators.note: Mr Geller is placed in the situation made by the money letters, sitting between them

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for a pound sterling, from the Latin libra
D is the old abbreviation for a penny, from the Latin denarius
Uri Geller is the famous spoon-bending entertainer

explanation.surface: A spoon-bender finds himself in a long-odds position worthy of a sensational stage play.
explanation.walkthrough: The pound and penny give L and D; 'in' sets URI between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Lurid means sensational and shocking, the vivid excess typical of melodrama.

clue.text: "No fustian about church-yards, no — tales" (E. A. Poe, The Premature Burial)

definitions.text: "No fustian about church-yards, no — tales" (E. A. Poe, The Premature Burial)

parts.words: "No fustian about church-yards, no — tales" (E. A. Poe, The Premature Burial)
parts.note: the gap in Poe's sentence wants a word for a bogey or object of groundless fear

explanation.definitionFit: Poe's narrator rejects bogey tales, a word for imaginary terrors that frighten children.

clue.text: He who thus manages disbelief may procure poetic faith, thought Coleridge

definitions.text: He who thus manages disbelief may procure poetic faith, thought Coleridge

parts.words: He who thus manages disbelief may procure poetic faith, thought Coleridge
parts.note: Coleridge's Biographia Literaria speaks of the willing setting-aside of disbelief that constitutes poetic faith

explanation.definitionFit: Coleridge's phrase is the willing suspension of disbelief, so the verb is to hold disbelief in abeyance.

clue.text: Reportedly sacerdotal dramatist from Bradford

indicators.note: something reported is passed on by word of mouth, so the spoken sound of the next word is wanted

parts.note: sacerdotal means of or like a member of the clergy

explanation.surface: A playwright from Yorkshire is said to have had a clerical air.
explanation.walkthrough: J. B. Priestley, author of An Inspector Calls, was born in Bradford, a city in Yorkshire.
explanation.definitionFit: J. B. Priestley, born in Bradford, wrote the play An Inspector Calls.

clue.text: Indian music article in tatters

indicators.note: the article is put in the word for tatters, inside its letters

parts.note: tatters are torn scraps of cloth, rags
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: Some music from the subcontinent is being played by someone dressed in rags.
explanation.definitionFit: Ragas are the melodic frameworks for improvisation in Indian classical music, plural like the definition.

clue.text: A small-part actor is worth one more run

definitions.meaning: a film walk-on performer with no lines
in cricket a run added to the score without being scored off the bat, such as a wide

explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, a run conceded by a wide or no-ball is added without the batsman hitting it.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses share the idea of something additional: a supplementary performer and a bonus run.

clue.text: These melodies of Keats were sweeter

definitions.text: These melodies of Keats were sweeter

parts.words: These melodies of Keats were sweeter
parts.note: Keats's Ode on a Grecian Urn: heard melodies are sweet, but those unheard are sweeter

explanation.definitionFit: The unheard melodies of Keats's ode are those no ear can catch, which is what the adjective means.

clue.text: Can theme I've totally recomposed be seen as success?

indicators.note: music recomposed is written afresh, so these letters are rearranged, 'totally' meaning all of them

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
the contraction with its apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: A composer asks whether rewriting a whole musical theme counts as a triumph.
explanation.walkthrough: 'totally recomposed' tells you to rearrange every letter of CAN THEME I'VE.
explanation.definitionFit: An achievement is an accomplishment, something won through effort, as a success is.

clue.text: Observe chemist suggesting pseudonym for Victorian novelist

parts.note: to mark something is to notice or observe it
Ernest Rutherford won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his work on radioactivity

explanation.surface: Note how a scientist's name hints at the alias of a nineteenth-century writer.
explanation.walkthrough: Mark Rutherford was the pen name of William Hale White; Ernest Rutherford, though a physicist, received the Nobel Prize for Chemistry.
explanation.definitionFit: William Hale White published The Autobiography of Mark Rutherford and later novels under that assumed name.

clue.text: Suggested element of wall, also descriptive of rude mechanicals?

definitions.meaning: in A Midsummer Night's Dream the actor playing Wall wears plaster and loam to suggest one
Shakespeare's rude mechanicals are the crude amateur company of workmen putting on a play

explanation.walkthrough: Snout, playing Wall, says this loam and plaster show he is the wall; the workmen-actors are an unpolished cast.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names a coarse wall plaster, and read as two words it describes an unpolished troupe of players.

clue.text: Sounds like sort of woman associated with O'Hara

indicators.note: the phrase tells us the next word is to be heard rather than spelt

parts.note: a scarlet woman is the old phrase for an immoral one

explanation.surface: A certain kind of woman is linked by name to a family in Gone with the Wind.
explanation.walkthrough: Scarlett O'Hara is the heroine of Gone with the Wind.
explanation.definitionFit: Scarlett is the first name of Margaret Mitchell's heroine, Miss O'Hara.

clue.text: 14 portrays Brontë heroine by the gorse

parts.note: Catherine Earnshaw is the heroine of Emily Brontë's Wuthering Heights
furze is another name for gorse, the spiny yellow-flowered shrub

explanation.surface: A novelist depicts a moorland heroine standing beside some gorse bushes.
explanation.walkthrough: 14 is MARK RUTHERFORD, whose 1893 novel bears this title; 'portrays' points to the book's subject.
explanation.definitionFit: Mark Rutherford's novel is named after its heroine, so this is whom that writer depicts.

clue.text: Its ranks could scarce forbear to cheer

definitions.text: Its ranks could scarce forbear to cheer

parts.words: Its ranks could scarce forbear to cheer
parts.note: Macaulay's Horatius: even the enemy ranks of an Italian region could scarce forbear to cheer

explanation.definitionFit: In Macaulay's Lays of Ancient Rome the opposing Etruscan army belongs to this Italian region.

clue.text: The delightful Miss Dobson — inspirer of mass sacrifice to Isis

definitions.text: The delightful Miss Dobson — inspirer of mass sacrifice to Isis

parts.words: The delightful Miss Dobson — inspirer of mass sacrifice to Isis
parts.note: in Max Beerbohm's novel the Oxford undergraduates drown themselves for love of Miss Dobson; the Isis is the Thames at Oxford

explanation.definitionFit: Beerbohm's heroine Miss Dobson causes Oxford's young men to throw themselves into the river for her.

clue.text: Pier at which Mr Turner, like Mr Piper, was "pretty unlucky with the weather"

definitions.text: Pier at which Mr Turner, like Mr Piper, was "pretty unlucky with the weather"

parts.words: Pier at which Mr Turner, like Mr Piper, was "pretty unlucky with the weather"
parts.note: Turner painted a stormy French harbour pier; George VI told John Piper he had been pretty unlucky with the weather

explanation.definitionFit: Turner's painting Calais Pier shows a storm-tossed crossing at the French port, as gloomy as Piper's skies.

clue.text: Lodge entrances with Shakespearean cross-dresser

parts.note: Thomas Lodge's prose romance, source of As You Like It, charms with the heroine who dresses as a young man

explanation.walkthrough: 'Lodge' is the Elizabethan writer Thomas Lodge, not a gatehouse; 'entrances' means enchants.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Lodge's romance is named for the heroine Shakespeare took for As You Like It, who disguises herself as Ganymede.

clue.text: Bloomer associated by Koestler with automaton

definitions.text: Bloomer associated by Koestler with automaton

parts.words: Bloomer associated by Koestler with automaton
parts.note: a bloomer is a flower here; Koestler's book on Asian mysticism pairs a water flower with the robot

explanation.definitionFit: Arthur Koestler's 1960 book is The ___ and the Robot, the gap a sacred water flower.

clue.text: Reed's composer a bit of a pill

definitions.text: Reed's composer a bit of a pill

parts.words: Reed's composer a bit of a pill
parts.note: Henry Reed's radio comedies feature a formidable woman composer whose surname means a pill, and she is a trying person

explanation.walkthrough: Henry Reed wrote BBC radio plays about the composer Hilda Tablet; a tablet is a pill.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry Reed's comic composer is Hilda Tablet, whose surname is another word for a pill.

clue.text: Carry out directions on part of play

parts.note: E and N are the compass directions east and north
an act is a main division of a play

explanation.surface: Stage directions tell actors what to perform in a section of the drama.
explanation.definitionFit: To enact a law or a scene is to put it into effect or perform it.

clue.text: Finest papyrus from upper region of Greece, we hear

indicators.note: what we hear is spoken, so the sound of the phrase is meant

parts.note: higher Attica, Attica being the region of Greece around Athens

explanation.surface: The best papyrus is said to come from the uplands of Greece.
explanation.walkthrough: Hieratica was the finest grade of papyrus, reserved for sacred texts; it sounds like 'higher Attica'.
explanation.definitionFit: Roman writers called the top grade of papyrus, kept for priestly texts, by this name.

clue.text: Whose hour described by Glyn?

parts.note: Elinor Glyn wrote a romantic novel titled with a possessive pronoun before Hour

explanation.definitionFit: Elinor Glyn's 1910 novel is ___ Hour, the gap a masculine possessive.

clue.text: Staff of Dionysus acquired ivy wreath

definitions.text: Staff of Dionysus acquired ivy wreath

parts.words: Staff of Dionysus acquired ivy wreath
parts.note: the wine god's rod was tipped with a pine cone and twined with ivy

explanation.definitionFit: The ritual wand carried by Dionysus and his maenads was wreathed in ivy and vine leaves.

clue.text: What are the Simpsons?

parts.note: the cartoon family has four members besides the baby? read here as a set of four

explanation.definitionFit: A tetrad is a group of four, as a family of four might be counted.
